title: Double Eye Whammy and Freddie King's San Jose
summary: Freddie King took his Rick record home and recorded San Jose, a hit, and later a vocal Double Eye Whammy, without payment.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Okay, now, there's another record that I wrote and recorded with Rick Records.
Freddie King came down here, and he was on the cause. He was living on the causeway at Marino's Motel, and he and I got to be buddy buddies for a while. He was here because his cause broke down.
And I gave him one of my records that just came out on Rick. Freddie King went back to Dallas, and he recorded a tune called San Jose. And if you listen to San Jose and listen to Double I Whammy.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you.
Reel number three, April the 23rd, 1986 with Tommy Richland. So we're talking about William and Freddie King.

This was a tune I recorded with Rick Records, and it was a good thing. It was one of the few tunes that I did with my band, my arrangement, my song, you know, the whole thing. But anyway, this was my band. It was the original, one of the Untouchables things that we did. And it had a good sound. And while Freddie King was in town, his car had broke down. He was living on the causeway at Marino's Motel. I'm a saxophone player in my band.
And he owned the hotel hotel?

Yeah, Marino owned his hotel. He's still there. He's still here, incidentally. Well anyway, Freddie King and I got to talking. We got friendly. And I told him about my tune. He didn't bring me a record. So he brought, he came to my house, listened to it. He said, I'm going to take this record back to Dallas. And he took the record back to Dallas with him. And lo and behold, Freddie King recorded my tune as an instrumental. And the title was San Jose. And if you listen to the two tunes they are exactly, he played exactly what I'm singing. That chick is a walking dog. I did, did, did, did, did, did, did. Okay, he played. And it made number 17 Billboard chart and whatever on the other book, in the book. In the book. Well, I never heard. Now, I don't know if Ruffino was paying any money. I don't know if they got it. Evidently. Something had to, you know, because the record was too big for them not to have gotten anything. It was in, well, anyway, my attorneys had that. Now, Freddie King also recorded Double Eye Whammy of mine. I mean, the girl from Cookemona. He did that. Now, that's on an album I have around here somewhere. But I didn't know Freddie King did. And they tell me he did a few other things from people from down here. In other words, all of his hits were the things that he got from down here in New Orleans. Check that out, Freddie King.
Did Freddie stay here for a long period of time?

Now, he would come in. He would always come in and play, you know. Now, he was pretty big. He was a white artist. Freddie King would show up in town and do his thing and listen and find what the hottest record and get on back to Dallas and record. Now, he got in touch with me and told me he was going to do Double Eye Whammy again. And he did a singing version. Evidently, I was on a local label in Dallas. I got a few statements and that's all I ever got. I couldn't remember, you know. But that was it. But anyway, that was a big record and I had my lawyers checking into that to see if we could come across any money. Because that was 1966, so that ain't that long ago. Yeah.
